BALANCE EVENTS B001-B120 - STATIC AND MIXER FORMS (draft for the owner, 2026-11-15)
New events written to even out how often each kind of outcome happens. Same layout as OWNER_EDITED_315.txt:
the static event, then its mixer seed. Every ending within a choice is equally likely.
NOT in the patcher. They go in only when you say GO.

How to read this (same as the 315):
- (Name)/(name) is the main villager. With two villagers, (name1) and (name2). Pronouns follow (name) or (name1);
  a pronoun for (name2) is written (name2: he/she), (name2: his/her) and so on.
- (new name) is a random default name the game picks. (award) is the amount actually given.
- Food and tech amounts follow that game's own island-event ranges: small = half, normal, large = twice.
- A permanent disability lowers health by the amount given, adds the dislike named, and gives the "old" head look.
- A DUPLICATE has the same looks but new likes, dislikes and skills, and a different name. A CLONE is an exact copy
  (looks, likes, dislikes, skills) with a different name. "CLONE OF (name) (2)" makes two clones, each named differently.
- Pregnancy: the carrier is born female and 18 or older, with the partner named, unless the line says (ANY BIRTH SEX),
  used only for magic the couple asked for, or for caring for a found baby. Pregnancies come only to villagers who
  already wanted a child.
- Deaths count as "Unknown causes" unless the line says otherwise. Games: all five unless the heading says otherwise.
  In New Believers, the people outside the faith are Isolans, and new arrivals are Isolans who choose to join.
- "?" names come only from a bump on the head, a fall, a fever or memory-taking magic.
- In MIXER seeds, {this|that|other} means the mixer picks one at random.

==============================================================================
B001. The Undertow   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (name1) one villager aged 14 or older (not protected); (name2) a fisher, another villager aged 18 or older (not protected). In VV5, believers.
EVENT TEXT
(Name1) loves swimming more than anything, and today (he/she) has swum out further than ever, past the reef, where the water turns from green to a deep, cold blue. (Name2), the head fisher, is mending nets on the beach and has told (him/her) twice already that the tide is turning.
Halfway back, (name1) feels it. The water pulls at (his/her) legs, gently at first, then like a hand around (his/her) ankle, dragging (him/her) out towards the open sea. The shore is getting smaller.
(Name1) could fight across the current, the way (he/she) was taught as a child, or wave and shout and hope (name2) looks up from the nets in time.

Choice A: Swim Across the Current
Choice B: Wave and Shout for Help

CHOICE A: SWIM ACROSS THE CURRENT
First popup: (Name1) stops fighting the pull and turns sideways, swimming along the beach instead of towards it, the way the old fishers always said. (His/Her) arms burn. A wave slaps (him/her) in the face, and then another...

Ending A1 -- PAST THE REEF. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name1) DISAPPEARS (no grave)
(Name2) looks up from the nets and sees nothing but water. (He/She) shouts, and the whole village comes running. The canoes go out before anyone has finished asking what happened, and they search until dark, and again at first light, calling (name1)'s name across the water until their voices give out. They find nothing, not even (his/her) shell necklace. The sea has kept (him/her). Every evening for a long time afterwards, someone sits on the beach and watches the place past the reef where the water turns blue.

Ending A2 -- THE LONG WAY ROUND. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name1) loses the like of swimming (story only: the like has no effect in any game)
It works, slowly. (Name1) crawls up onto the sand a long way down the beach, coughing up half the lagoon, and lies there until (name2) comes jogging over with a gourd of water and a face like thunder. "Twice," (name2) says. "I told you twice." (Name1) still goes into the water after that, but only to wash, and only up to the knees. The joy of it is gone. When the children race out to the reef, (he/she) watches from the shore and counts them all back in.

CHOICE B: WAVE AND SHOUT FOR HELP
First popup: (Name1) throws an arm up and yells (name2)'s name as loud as (his/her) aching lungs will let (him/her). The wind takes most of it. On the beach, (name2) stops mending, and lifts (name2: his/her) head...

Ending B1 -- THE FISHER'S ROPE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name2) gains 10 to 20 in (name2: his/her) best skill
(Name2) is in a canoe before the shout has finished. (He/She) paddles out along the edge of the current, never into it, throws a coil of rope with a float tied to the end, and hauls (name1) in hand over hand like the biggest catch of (name2: his/her) life. Back on the beach, the village crowds round (name2) and asks how (name2: he/she) knew exactly where to paddle. (Name2) shrugs and goes back to the nets, but (name2: he/she) teaches the trick to every young fisher who will listen, and gets better at it every time.

Ending B2 -- TOO FAR OUT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name1) DIES (a grave)
(Name2) hears, and is in the canoe in moments, paddling harder than (name2: he/she) has ever paddled. But the current is faster than any canoe. By the time (name2) reaches the place where (name1) was, the water is empty and smooth. The fishers find (name1) the next morning, washed against the far rocks, and carry (him/her) home wrapped in a sail. The village buries (him/her) above the beach, facing the reef. (Name2) mends nets alone for a long time after that, and nobody tries to talk (name2: him/her) out of it.

MIXER SEED B001
Premise: (Name1) has swum out past the reef, where the water turns deep and cold, and the current takes hold of (his/her) legs while (name2), the head fisher, mends nets on the beach.
Roles:
  swimmer: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
  fisher: another villager aged 18 or older (not protected)
Approaches: Swim Across the Current | Wave and Shout for Help | Float and Wait | Swim Straight for Shore

  - The canoes search until dark and again at first light. The sea has kept (name1). [answers: Swim Across the Current, Swim Straight for Shore] [mood: sad] [EFFECT: (name1) DISAPPEARS (no grave)]
  - (Name1) crawls up far down the beach, and never loves swimming again. [answers: Swim Across the Current, Float and Wait] [mood: warm] [EFFECT: (name1) loses the like of swimming (story only: the like has no effect in any game)]
  - (Name2) paddles along the edge of the current and hauls (name1) in like the biggest catch of (name2: his/her) life. [answers: Wave and Shout for Help, Float and Wait] [mood: warm] [EFFECT: (name2) gains 10 to 20 in (name2: his/her) best skill]
  - By the time (name2) reaches the place, the water is empty. The fishers bring (name1) home the next morning. [answers: Wave and Shout for Help, Swim Straight for Shore] [mood: sad] [EFFECT: (name1) DIES (a grave)]
  - (Name1) lies back and floats until the current lets go, then drifts in on the evening waves, freezing and furious with (himself/herself). [answers: Float and Wait] [mood: warm] [EFFECT: none]
Flavour lines:
  - Past the reef the water turns from green to a deep, cold blue.
  - (Name2) has said twice already that the tide is turning.
  - The shore is getting smaller.

B002. The Three-Day Fever   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected) who is ill; (healer name) the village's best healer. In VV5, believers.
EVENT TEXT
(Name) has had a fever for three days. (He/She) is burning hot and shivering at the same time, and keeps talking to people who aren't in the hut. On the third night (he/she) sits up and asks (healer name), the healer, why the roof is full of fish.
(Healer name) has tried every leaf in the basket. There is one thing left: a bitter red root that grows only on the cliff, that the old healers used when nothing else worked. It breaks a fever fast, but it can also take things with it, and nobody is sure what.
Should (healer name) use the root, or keep (name) cool and wait out the night?

Choice A: Use the Red Root
Choice B: Keep (Him/Her) Cool and Wait

CHOICE A: USE THE RED ROOT
First popup: (Healer name) grinds the root into a paste that smells like rust and wet stone, and spoons it between (name)'s teeth. (Name) swallows, makes a face like (he/she) has bitten a beetle, and falls straight asleep...

Ending A1 -- THE FEVER BREAKS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: illness cured; LOSES NAME (name becomes "?")
By morning the fever is gone and (name) is sitting up, cool and hungry and asking for food. Then (healer name) asks how (he/she) is feeling, calling (him/her) by name, and (name) looks blank. "Who?" The root took the fever, and it took (his/her) name along with it. Everything else is still there: (his/her) friends, (his/her) work, the way (he/she) likes (his/her) fish. Just not the name. The village tries saying it to (him/her) for a week. It never sticks. In the end, everyone just calls (him/her) "?" and (he/she) answers to it cheerfully.

Ending A2 -- BITTER AND BETTER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: illness cured; loses the dislike of medicine (all five games: takes the Healing job as often as anyone)
The fever breaks before dawn, soaking the sleeping mat. (Name) wakes up weak as a newborn bird and very, very thirsty. The root has a strange aftertaste that stays for days. (Name) has always hated the bitter smell of herbs and the clink of remedy bowls, but after three days in the healers' hut, they have become a comfort. "I nearly died," (he/she) says, when someone asks why (he/she) now lingers by the healers' hut. "It puts things in perspective." (Healer name) writes down the dose very carefully, and hides the rest of the root.

CHOICE B: KEEP (HIM/HER) COOL AND WAIT
First popup: (Healer name) puts the root away. (Healer name: He/She) sits by the mat all night with a bowl of cool water and a cloth, wiping (name)'s face, listening to (name) argue with the fish on the roof...

Ending B1 -- THE LONG NIGHT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: illness cured
It is a long night. Twice (healer name) nearly gets up for the root. But somewhere before dawn, (name)'s breathing slows and evens out, and the heat goes out of (his/her) skin like a fire burning down. In the morning (he/she) is weak, and grumpy, and absolutely fine. "Why is everyone staring at me?" (he/she) asks. (Healer name), who has not slept at all, goes home and sleeps until the next afternoon.

Ending B2 -- NOT YET. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The fever hangs on through the night, and the next day, and the next. It doesn't get worse. It doesn't get better either. (Name) sleeps most of the time and complains the rest. (Healer name) keeps the cool cloths coming and the root in its basket, and the rest of the healers take turns sitting up. It is a slow recovery, when it comes, and nobody is in a hurry to call it one.

MIXER SEED B002

B003. The Basket in the Mangroves   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 18 or older (not protected), any birth sex. (name2) is (name)'s partner, if (he/she) has one. In VV5, a believer.
EVENT TEXT
(Name) is gathering crabs among the mangrove roots when (he/she) hears a thin, hiccupping cry. Wedged between two roots, just above the waterline, is a woven basket with a baby inside, red-faced and furious and very much alive. The basket is good work, tightly plaited, the kind of thing someone makes with care.
There's a canoe track in the mud, already filling with water, leading out towards the channel. Whoever brought the baby here came by sea, and not long ago.
(Name) lifts the basket out. The baby stops crying and grabs (his/her) thumb. Should (name) take the baby home, or wait here in case someone comes back?

Choice A: Take the Baby Home
Choice B: Wait for Someone to Come Back

CHOICE A: TAKE THE BABY HOME
First popup: (Name) tucks the basket against (his/her) chest and wades back through the roots, talking to the baby the whole way about crabs, and mud, and how they're nearly home...

Ending A1 -- "I FOUND YOU, SO YOU'RE MINE." Chance 50%. EFFECT: (ANY BIRTH SEX) (name) becomes NURSING the foundling baby (single parent)
The whole village comes to look. The baby looks back, unimpressed. The elders ask around, and the fishers watch the channel for days, but no one comes looking. "I found you," (name) tells the baby, "so I'll take care of you." And (he/she) does, every night and every day, through the crying and the feeding and the sleepless nights, with the basket hung over the door so the baby can see where (he/she) came from one day.

Ending A2 -- THE WHOLE VILLAGE HELPS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (ANY BIRTH SEX) (name) becomes NURSING the foundling baby, with (his/her) partner if (he/she) has one
(Name) gets the baby home, and the baby screams for an hour straight, and (name) panics. Then (name2) comes in, and (healer name) comes in, and somebody's grandmother comes in with a sling and a pot of mashed fruit, and suddenly there are six people in the hut, all with opinions. By nightfall the baby is fed, clean and fast asleep on (name)'s chest. "We'll take turns," says (name2). And they do.

CHOICE B: WAIT FOR SOMEONE TO COME BACK
First popup: (Name) sits down on a dry root with the basket on (his/her) knees and waits, watching the channel, rocking the baby whenever (he/she) starts to fuss. The tide comes in. The sun starts to drop...

Ending B1 -- A CANOE AT DUSK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW VILLAGERS (two adults) arrive and stay, with their baby
Just before dark, a canoe comes slipping back up the channel. Two exhausted people are in it, soaked to the skin, and when they see the basket they start crying before the canoe touches the mud. Their island had a sickness, and they had left the baby somewhere sheltered while they went back for their things, and then the tide turned and they got lost in the channels. (Name) walks them all back to the village. They decide to stay.

Ending B2 -- NOBODY COMES. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Nobody comes. When the stars come out, (name) carries the baby back to the village, where the elders and the healers take over. Within a week, a couple who have been hoping for a child for years have taken the baby in, and (name) is the baby's favourite visitor. (He/She) never quite stops watching the channel, though.

B004. The Pool Under the Moon Rock   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected). In VV5, a believer.
EVENT TEXT
High in the hills there's a pool that the elders call the Moon Pool, because of the pale rock that hangs over it. The story goes that the rock fell from the sky long ago, and that its dust in the water makes the pool "remember" whoever looks into it. Most people think it's a story for keeping children away from a deep pool.
(Name) has come up anyway, on a dare. The water is perfectly still and shines with a faint, milky light even in the shade. When (he/she) leans over, the reflection is a little too sharp, like a carving of (him/her) rather than a picture.
(Name)'s friends are waiting at the bottom of the hill to hear what happened. Should (he/she) touch the water, or leave it alone?

Choice A: Touch the Water
Choice B: Drop a Stone In

CHOICE A: TOUCH THE WATER
First popup: (Name) dips one finger in. The water is warm, warmer than skin. The milky light gathers around (his/her) finger and climbs up (his/her) hand like a glove...

Ending A1 -- TWO MORE OF ME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: CLONE OF (name) (2), named (new name) and (new name)
The pool bulges, and {#made:one person climbs|two people climb|three people climb} out of it, dripping and blinking. {#made:The newcomer is|Both of them are|All three are} (name), down to the scar on (his/her) knee and the way (he/she) hums when nervous. They like what (name) likes and hate what (name) hates, and they argue about it with (name) all the way down the hill. The village decides that everyone needs a name of their own, and {#made:the newcomer becomes (new name)|the newcomers become (new name) and (new name)|the newcomers get names of their own}. They take it well. They take everything exactly the way (name) would.

Ending A2 -- ONE MORE OF ME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: CLONE of (name), named (new name); joins the village
A single figure rises out of the pool, (name) exactly, down to the last eyelash. It looks at (name), (name) looks at it, and they both say "Oh no," at the same moment, in the same voice. The friends at the bottom of the hill scream when two of (name) come walking down. The newcomer takes the name (new name), moves into the empty hut by the woodpile, and the two of them finish each other's sentences so often it drives the rest of the village mad.

CHOICE B: DROP A STONE IN
First popup: (Name) picks up a pebble and drops it into the middle of the pool. The ripples don't spread like ripples should. They gather, and fold, and take a shape...

Ending B1 -- NOT QUITE ME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: DUPLICATE of (name), named (new name); joins the village
Something climbs out where the stone went in. It has (name)'s face and (name)'s hair, but the stone broke the pool's memory, and it remembered only the outside. It is nothing like (name) inside. It loves the work (name) hates, laughs at different jokes and wants to know everything about everything. The village takes a while to stop calling it by the wrong name. It chooses (new name), and is soon the most popular person in the hut-building crew.

Ending B2 -- JUST A DEEP POOL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The ripples settle. The milky light fades out of the water, slowly, like a lamp being turned down, and the pool is just a pool, dark and deep and cold. (Name) waits a long time. Nothing happens. (He/She) walks down to (his/her) friends and tells them it was nothing. Then (he/she) never goes up the hill again, and changes the subject whenever anyone asks why.

B005. The Blessing Stones   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: two villagers aged 18 or older who are partners: (name1) born female, and (name2) (neither protected). In VV5, believers.
EVENT TEXT
(Name1) and (name2) have been hoping for a baby for a long time. They don't talk about it much, but everyone knows, the way everyone in a small village knows everything.
(Healer name), the oldest healer, finds them one evening and presses two smooth river stones into their hands, warm from (healer name: his/her) pocket. "My grandmother gave these to me," (healer name: he/she) says. "Put them under your sleeping mat, and drink the leaf tea I'll leave you. It might do nothing. But it might not." Then (healer name: he/she) goes away before they can thank (healer name: him/her).
They look at each other. Should they try the stones and the tea, or just let things happen in their own time?

Choice A: Try the Stones and the Tea
Choice B: Let Things Happen in Their Own Time

CHOICE A: TRY THE STONES AND THE TEA
First popup: The tea tastes of grass and something sweet. The stones go under the mat. (Name1) and (name2) lie awake for a long time that night, holding hands, feeling a little silly and a little hopeful...

Ending A1 -- ONE BABY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name1) is PREGNANT, with (name2) as the other parent (one baby)
A few weeks later, (name1) can't stand the smell of fish, and then can't stop eating mangoes, and then (healer name) comes round with a knowing smile. A baby is expected. (Name2) runs round the whole village telling everybody, including people who already know, including the pigs. The stones go back to (healer name), who puts them in (healer name: his/her) pocket and says, "Well. It might not have been the stones."

Ending A2 -- MORE THAN THEY BARGAINED FOR. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name1) is PREGNANT, with (name2) as the other parent (twins or triplets, if the game allows)
A baby is expected. Then, as the weeks go by, (healer name) listens to (name1)'s belly for a long time, and frowns, and listens again, and starts counting on (healer name: his/her) fingers. "{#babies:One. Just the one. I was sure there were more|Two. You'll want a bigger sleeping mat|Three. You'll want a much bigger sleeping mat}," (healer name: he/she) says at last. (Name2) has to sit down. The village starts building {#babies:a cradle|two cradles|three cradles}.

CHOICE B: LET THINGS HAPPEN IN THEIR OWN TIME
First popup: They thank (healer name) the next day, and give the stones back. "We'd like to just see what happens," (name1) says. (Healer name) nods as if (healer name: he/she) expected nothing else...

Ending B1 -- IN ITS OWN TIME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name1) is PREGNANT, with (name2) as the other parent (one baby, after a short wait)
They stop counting the days. They go fishing together, and build a new shelf, and argue cheerfully about where to put it. And one morning, a few months later, (name1) wakes up feeling sick as a dog and knows, before (healer name) even says it. A baby is expected. "No stones," (name2) tells everyone proudly. "No tea. Just us."

Ending B2 -- A FULL HOUSE ANYWAY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
No baby comes that season, or the next. Instead, (name1) and (name2) somehow become the couple every child in the village runs to: for a story, for a scraped knee, for a place to hide from chores. Their hut is never quiet. "We'll see," (name1) says, when anyone asks, and means it. Their life is already full.

Choice B: Wait for a Still Night

Afterwards, even the people who always kept away from village gatherings find they want to be among everyone.

B041. The Dance of Shared Hearts   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: two villagers aged 14 or older (not protected) who are friends. In VV5, believers.
EVENT TEXT
At the midsummer dance there's one old step that nobody does anymore: two dancers circle each other, closer and closer, palm to palm, and then spin round each other three times without letting go. The elders call it the dance of shared hearts. Their grandparents stopped doing it because, they say, "sometimes the hearts get shared too well."
(Name1) and (name2) have learned it in secret from an old song, and tonight, with the drums going and the fire high, they're standing palm to palm in the middle of the circle. Everyone has gone quiet.
Should they spin all three times, or stop at two and bow?

Choice A: Spin All Three Times
Choice B: Stop at Two and Bow

CHOICE A: SPIN ALL THREE TIMES
First popup: One. Two. On the third spin the drums seem to stop, though the drummers are still drumming, and the fire leans towards them like a listening face...

Ending A1 -- SHARED TOO WELL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent)
They stop, dizzy, and let go, and (name1) staggers backwards in (name2)'s body. The whole circle gasps. The elders nod grimly: shared too well. The two of them go home to each other's huts that night, too stunned to argue, and in the morning they're still swapped. They're good friends, so it could be worse. They do teach the step to nobody, ever.

Ending A2 -- THE CIRCLE JOINS IN. Chance 50%. EFFECT: every villager is happier (stock island-event effect)
Nothing strange happens, except that it's beautiful. When they stop, the whole circle roars, and suddenly everyone wants to learn, and the elders, who said they'd forgotten it, are out in the middle showing people how. The dance goes on till dawn. The old step is back.

Smoke them out with a fire of bitter leaves, which works but smells so bad the village will have to sleep on the beach for three nights. Or replace every hollow post with ironwood, which termites can't eat, but which means a lot of work for everyone.

Choice A: Smoke Them Out
Choice B: Replace the Posts with Ironwood

CHOICE A: SMOKE THEM OUT

It takes two weeks of aching backs and blistered hands, but at the end of it every hut in the village stands on ironwood. The termites move out in disgust, and go and live in a dead tree in the forest, where they belong. "Built to last," says (name), knocking on a post. It rings like a bell.

Two weeks of carrying ironwood is too much for (name). By the end of it, every post is replaced and the village is safe, but (name) is so sick of posts, hauling, knocking and wood that (he/she) hands the job over to the next best builder and takes up fishing. "I've built enough," (he/she) says. "Let someone else knock on things."

EVENT TEXT

The old story is that two people who look into the pond at that moment "see each other as the moon does," and some of them never quite get back to their own side.
(Name1) and (name2) have climbed up to see it. The moon is rising. Its reflection is creeping across the black water towards the place where they're kneeling, side by side.

Ending A1 -- THE OTHER SIDE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent)

Choice B: The Cold Pool

(Name) climbs out with a younger face, smooth and bright. The aches come back by the time (he/she) reaches the village. "The warm sister wanted to be young," says an elder. "She didn't say anything about knees."

CHOICE B: THE COLD POOL

Ending B2 -- JUST COLD. Chance 50%. EFFECT: the "old" head look

# BALANCE EVENTS B121-B240 (120 new events, writer 2 of 3)
##############################################################################
New island events written to even out the outcome kinds (owner: every outcome kind in about 60 endings across
the 315 rewritten events plus the new ones). Same style guide and layout as OWNER_EDITED_315.txt: the static event,
then its MIXER SEED. Draft for the owner; nothing ships until approved.

How to read this (as in the 315):
- (Name)/(name) is the main villager; with two, (name1) and (name2). A pronoun for (name2) is written (name2: he/she).
- Side characters use role tokens: (healer name), (builder name), (fisher name), (elder name), (child name) and so on.
- (new name) / (new name 2) are random default names. (award) is the amount actually given.
- {#babies:a baby|twins|triplets} and {#made:...} are count tokens the engine fills in after the effect runs, so an
  ending reads right whether the game makes one baby, twins or triplets.
- Every ending within a choice is equally likely (50% each).
- Like and dislike effects name the per-game word that does what the story means, from likes_dislikes.json, and say
  in which games that word changes behaviour and where it is story only.
- Pregnancy carriers are born female and 18 or older, with the partner named, unless the line says (ANY BIRTH SEX)
  (only for caring for a found baby). In New Believers, people outside the faith are Isolans; VV2 totems are never picked.

B121. The Fever Tea   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older who is a healer or has some Healing (not protected); (name2) is a sick villager, if there is one
EVENT TEXT
A fever has been going round the village for a week. It starts with a scratchy throat and ends with three days on a mat, sweating through every blanket in the hut. (Name2) has had it the longest, and the healers have run out of ideas and most of their patience.
Late one night, (name) finds a plant growing beside the healers' hut that was not there yesterday: a little purple herb with leaves shaped like spoons. (Healer name), the oldest healer, squints at it and says (his/her) grandmother used to brew it for fevers, "or possibly for warts. One or the other." Nobody else has ever seen it. It smells like pepper and wet stone.
(Name) holds the leaves over the boiling pot. Should (he/she) brew the tea and try it, or wait until (healer name) remembers which one it was?

Choice A: Brew the Tea
Choice B: Wait for (Healer Name) to Remember

CHOICE A: BREW THE TEA
First popup: (Name) drops the leaves into the pot. The water turns the colour of a bruise and starts to hum, very faintly, like a bee trapped in a gourd. (He/She) pours out a cup for (name2), then, after a moment's thought, takes a sip first...

Ending A1 -- THE FEVER BREAKS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name2)'s illness is cured; every healer gains 10 Healing
(Name2) drinks the whole cup, pulls a face like a child eating a lemon, and falls asleep. By morning the fever is gone. By noon (name2) is up and complaining about being hungry. The healers crowd round the pot, writing down how many leaves, how long, how hot, and argue happily about it all day. "Fevers," says (healer name) at last, very pleased. "It was definitely fevers."

Ending A2 -- THE SIP. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name) LOSES NAME (name becomes "?"), from the fever-dream the tea brings on; (name2)'s illness is cured
The tea works on (name2) at once. It also works on (name), who only had a sip, and spends the night in a burning, swimming dream about walking through a village where every hut has a door but no names on anything. In the morning (name)'s fever is gone, and so is (his/her) name. (He/She) can remember the dream perfectly, and (his/her) own name not at all. The village calls (him/her) "?" until it comes back. It does not come back. "Warts," says (healer name) gloomily. "It might have been for warts."

CHOICE B: WAIT FOR (HEALER NAME) TO REMEMBER
First popup: (Name) sets the leaves down carefully on a flat stone. "Think," (he/she) says. "Fevers or warts?" (Healer name) sits down, closes (his/her) eyes, and thinks for so long that (name) wonders if (he/she) has fallen asleep...

Ending B1 -- GRANDMOTHER'S SONG. Chance 50%. EFFECT: all sick villagers are cured (stock island-event effect)
At last (healer name) opens (his/her) eyes and starts to hum a song (his/her) grandmother sang while she brewed: two handfuls of leaves, boil it twice, let it cool under the moon. They do it exactly as the song says. Every sick villager in the village gets a cup, and by the end of the week the fever has gone from every hut. The purple herb is never seen beside the healers' hut again, though they look for it every spring.

Ending B2 -- TOO LONG. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
By the time (healer name) has remembered, the leaves have wilted on the stone and turned black and slimy. "Fevers," (he/she) says triumphantly, and then looks at the stone. "Oh." The fever runs its course the slow way. (Name2) gets better on (his/her) own, one long week later, and tells everyone (he/she) would have tried anything, even wart tea.

B122. The Night the Roofs Flew   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older who has some Building (not protected); the rest of the village
EVENT TEXT
The wind came in after dark and did not knock. By midnight it had lifted the thatch off half the huts in the village and thrown it into the jungle like a child throwing leaves. By dawn it had gone, leaving a clear blue sky and a village full of people standing in their huts looking up at it.
(Name) has the most Building in the village, so everyone is looking at (him/her). (Builder name), the second-best builder, is looking at (him/her) hardest of all. The thatch is scattered for half a mile. There are fresh palm fronds in the grove, but cutting enough will take days.
Should (name) gather the whole village and rebuild today, or tell everyone to wait for the dry fronds to be fetched back from the jungle?

Choice A: Rebuild Together Today
Choice B: Fetch Back the Old Thatch

CHOICE A: REBUILD TOGETHER TODAY
First popup: (Name) climbs onto the nearest bare roof frame and shouts until everyone is listening. Children are sent for fronds, the strongest villagers to the grove with knives, and everyone else is handed a coil of rope and told to hold on to it and not let go...

Ending A1 -- MANY HANDS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: the damaged huts are repaired (stock island-event effect); every villager gains 5 Building
It is the loudest day the village has had all year. Everyone is on a roof, or under one, or passing fronds up to someone on one. People who have never tied a knot in their lives learn three kinds by lunchtime. By sunset every hut has a roof again, a little greener than before and a lot more crooked. (Builder name) walks round all of them, pulling at the thatch and frowning. Then (he/she) says, grudgingly, "They'll do."

Ending A2 -- THE BEAM. Chance 50%. EFFECT: the damaged huts are repaired (stock island-event effect); (name) has a PERMANENT DISABILITY (health loss 30%); now dislikes wood (VV2-VV5: walks off building jobs; story only in VV1); "old" head look
The huts are almost finished when an old roof beam, cracked in the night, gives way under (name)'s feet. (He/She) falls hard, and the beam falls on top of (him/her). The healers do what they can. (Name)'s leg heals, but crooked, and (he/she) will walk with a stick from now on. The last roofs are finished by (builder name), who climbs down afterwards and sits beside (name) for a long time without saying anything. Then (he/she) says, "Your knots were better than mine." (Name) can't bear the creak of a roof frame after that, or the smell of fresh-cut thatch.

CHOICE B: FETCH BACK THE OLD THATCH
First popup: "Our old thatch is out there drying in the sun," (name) says. "No sense cutting new." The village spreads out into the jungle in a long line, picking up armfuls of thatch from bushes and branches and the tops of trees...

Ending B1 -- THE WHOLE ROOF. Chance 50%. EFFECT: the damaged huts are repaired (stock island-event effect); every villager is happier (stock island-event effect)
The wind turns out to have been oddly tidy. Whole roofs are found sitting in the clearings almost in one piece, like hats blown off in a gust. The villagers carry them back on their heads, four people to a roof, singing to keep in step. By evening every hut is roofed again. Someone finds the chief's lost sandal on the way, which nobody expected, and it is the best mood the village has been in all season.

Ending B2 -- FOUR DAYS OF SKY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (small amount)
The wind was not tidy. The thatch is in shreds, hanging from every branch, and most of it is too torn to use. It takes four days to cut new fronds and roof the huts again, and in the meantime it rains twice, onto everyone's beds and into the food store. "Should have rebuilt on the first day," says (builder name), to nobody in particular. Your village loses (award) food.

B123. The Still Pool Above the Falls   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 40 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
Above the waterfall there is a pool so still it looks like a hole in the ground filled with sky. The children are told never to swim in it, because it is very deep and very cold. The elders say it remembers everyone who has ever looked into it, and gives a little of what it remembers back.
(Name) has climbed up to fill a gourd, and kneels at the edge. In the water, (his/her) reflection looks back at (him/her) the way (he/she) looked twenty years ago: smooth cheeks, luscious hair, no tired lines at the eyes. The real (name) touches (his/her) face. The reflection doesn't.
Should (name) reach into the pool and take back what it remembers, or leave the pool alone?

Choice A: Reach Into the Pool
Choice B: Leave It Alone

CHOICE A: REACH INTO THE POOL
First popup: (Name) pushes (his/her) hand into the water. It is so cold it burns. The young reflection reaches up from below and takes (his/her) fingers, firmly, the way a parent takes a child's hand to cross a stream...

Ending A1 -- TEN YEARS BACK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: changes age (10 years younger); new look (the young head look)
When (name) pulls (his/her) hand out, the reflection has gone, and (name) can feel the difference all the way up (his/her) arm and into (his/her) back. (He/She) walks down the hill without stopping for breath once. In the village, people stare. "You look like you did when we were young," says (his/her) oldest friend, a little jealously. (Name) spends the evening doing all the things (his/her) knees wouldn't let (him/her) do last week, then sleeps like a stone.

Ending A2 -- ONLY THE FACE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: new look (the young head look)
The pool gives back the face, and only the face. (Name)'s knees still creak, (his/her) back still aches on the climb down, and (he/she) still needs a rest halfway. But the face that looks out of the cooking pot that evening is twenty years younger and very surprised. "It's a bit of a cheat," (name) admits to the healers. "Everything else still feels fifty." The children keep asking (him/her) to prove how old (he/she) is.

CHOICE B: LEAVE IT ALONE
First popup: (Name) sits back on (his/her) heels. There is something about the way the reflection is smiling that (he/she) doesn't like, as if it wants something too. (He/She) fills (his/her) gourd from the stream below instead, and gets up to go...

Ending B1 -- THE POOL TAKES ITS TURN. Chance 50%. EFFECT: new look (the "old" head look)
As (name) stands, a cold drop falls from the gourd and lands back in the pool. The pool takes it as a gift. By the time (name) reaches home, (his/her) hair has gone grey at the temples and (his/her) face has the soft, crumpled look of a grandparent. "Well, that's what I get for being polite," (he/she) says. The elders say the pool only ever takes what's offered, so (name) has nobody to blame but the gourd.

Ending B2 -- NO MORE RUNNING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name) loses the like of running (all five games: walks instead of running)
On the way down, (name) keeps thinking about the reflection's smile, and the cold of the water. That night (he/she) dreams of being pulled down into a deep, still pool, gently, by (his/her) own young hands. (He/She) wakes up with no wish to go anywhere near the water. (He/She) used to run down to the water every morning. Now (he/she) walks, slowly, and keeps well back from the waves.

B126. The Hollow Log   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
Deep in the jungle, where the trees are so tall the light comes down green, there is a fallen log big enough to walk through. (Name) is out gathering and stops to shout into it, just to see. "Hello!" (he/she) calls. From the far end comes back, in (his/her) own voice: "Hello yourself. Are you coming through, or shall I?"

Choice B: Wait at This End

CHOICE A: WALK THROUGH THE LOG

CHOICE B: WAIT AT THIS END

B127. The Festival Masks   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: two villagers aged 14 or older (not protected), (name1) and (name2)
EVENT TEXT
Every year before the harvest dance, (carver name), the mask-carver, sets out the old festival masks on a mat to be cleaned: wooden faces with shell eyes and grass hair, so old nobody knows who carved the first ones. There is a rule about them: each family wears only its own masks. Most of the village has forgotten why.
(Name1) and (name2) are supposed to be cleaning them. Instead they are trying them on, and they have each picked up the other family's mask. "Just for a moment," says (name2). "Just to see." The shell eyes catch the light.
(Carver name) is coming back up the path. Should they put the masks back quickly, or keep them on and see what happens?

Choice A: Keep Them On
Choice B: Put Them Back Quickly

CHOICE A: KEEP THEM ON
First popup: The masks are warm, warmer than wood should be, and they smell of old smoke and coconut oil. (Name1) looks across at (name2), and through the shell eyes, (name2) looks very strange, and very familiar...

Ending A1 -- THE WRONG FACES. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent)
When they pull the masks off, each of them is holding the other's mask in the other's hands. (Carver name) arrives, takes one look, and sits down heavily. "That's why," (he/she) says. "That's why the rule." The old carvings knew their families, and sent each of them home. Nobody knows how to undo it. (Name1) and (name2) spend the harvest dance in each other's bodies, stepping on each other's feet, and in the end they stop trying to change back.

Ending A2 -- THE SWAP AND THE SKILLS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent); each gains 10 to 20 in (his/her) best skill
They pull the masks off and find themselves looking out of each other's eyes. It is terrifying for about an hour. Then (name1) discovers that (name2)'s hands know things (name1)'s never did, and (name2) finds the same. Each of them is good at their own job and the other one's too. "It's a better deal than I expected," says (name2) at last, in (name1)'s voice. (Carver name) puts a lock on the mask chest anyway.

CHOICE B: PUT THEM BACK QUICKLY
First popup: They snatch the masks off and throw them back onto the mat just as (carver name) comes round the corner. Two masks land face up and two face down. (Carver name) looks at the mat, then at them, and raises one eyebrow very high...

Ending B1 -- THE NEW FACE PAINT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW LOOK for (name1) and (name2) (a painted face look)
"You've had them on," says (carver name). "Don't lie. The paint's come off on you." It has. Both of them have bright stripes of old festival paint across their cheeks and noses, red and white, the colours of the other family. It will not wash off. (Carver name) says it'll fade in a year or two. Everyone at the harvest dance thinks it looks wonderful, and three people ask how to get the same.

Ending B2 -- THE GRUDGE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name1) and (name2) each lose one dislike (at random)
(Carver name) makes them sit down and hear the story of why the families have separate masks. It turns out to be an old quarrel about a pig, generations ago, and nobody can even remember whose pig it was. (Name1) and (name2) laugh so hard at the pig that they forget to be scolded, and walk home feeling lighter. A few things they used to grumble about don't seem worth grumbling about any more.

(Name1) and (name2) were picking fruit on the hill when the storm came up, fast and black. The only shelter is the lightning tree. The rain is so heavy they can barely see each other, and the thunder is right on top of them.

Ending B2 -- SOAKED THROUGH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

B148. The Termite Year   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected); the builders
EVENT TEXT
Something has been eating the village. Quietly, for months. (Name) leans on a doorpost this morning and it crumbles under (his/her) hand like dry bread, full of tiny pale termites, all of them very busy. (Builder name), the head builder, checks every hut by noon: half the posts in the village are hollow.
There are two ways to deal with termites, the elders say. One is to smoke them out with burning herbs, which works but leaves the huts smelling for a year, and sometimes catches fire. The other is to tear out every post and replace it, which takes weeks and all the village's strength.
Should (name) smoke them out, or replace the posts?

Choice A: Smoke Them Out
Choice B: Replace the Posts

CHOICE A: SMOKE THEM OUT
First popup: (Name) and (builder name) light bundles of bitter herbs inside every hut, one by one, and stuff the doorways with wet leaves. Thick yellow smoke comes out of every crack. The village has to sleep on the beach...

Ending A1 -- THE SMELL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: the damaged huts are repaired (stock island-event effect); every builder gains 10 Building
The termites pour out of the posts in long pale rivers and march off into the jungle, deeply offended. The builders patch the worst posts while the smoke clears, and learn a great deal about how termites build, which they use to build better. The huts smell of bitter herbs for a year. Nobody gets bitten by mosquitoes for a year either, so it evens out.

Ending A2 -- THE RESEARCH HUT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: the damaged huts are repaired (stock island-event effect); tech loss (small amount)
The smoke works everywhere except the research hut, where a bundle of herbs rolls under a pile of notes and sets them smouldering. By the time anyone notices, a season of notes has gone up in yellow smoke. The termites are gone, and the huts are fixed, but the researchers walk round with grim faces for a week. Your villagers lose (award) tech points.

CHOICE B: REPLACE THE POSTS
First popup: The whole village goes into the jungle with axes and ropes. They cut new posts of hardwood, the kind termites hate, and drag them back one by one through the mud...

Ending B1 -- HARDWOOD. Chance 50%. EFFECT: the damaged huts are repaired (stock island-event effect); every villager gains 5 Building
It takes three weeks of mud, splinters and sore backs. By the end of it, everyone in the village knows how to set a post, even the children, who were meant to be fetching water. Every hut stands on new hardwood. (Builder name) says they'll last a hundred years. The termites come back the next season, look at the hardwood, and leave.

Ending B2 -- THE TREE THAT FELL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (builder name) DIES (a grave); the damaged huts are repaired (stock island-event effect)
On the last day, a great hardwood tree falls the wrong way. (Builder name) pushes two young villagers out of the way, and doesn't get out of the way (himself/herself). The village finishes the posts in silence. Every hut in the village stands on new posts now, and the last one, in the middle of the village, has (builder name)'s name carved on it.

EVENT TEXT
(Apprentice name), the healers' newest apprentice, has been trying to make a charm that helps two friends understand each other better. (He/She) found it on an old bark scroll, under a smudge. The smudge was important. Nobody knows that yet.
(Name1) and (name2) have been arguing for a month about whose turn it is to fetch water, and (apprentice name) has asked them, very nicely, to try the charm: a little bag of herbs each, worn round the neck for a night. "It'll help you see it from each other's side," (apprentice name) says. "That's what the scroll says. Mostly."
Should they wear the charms, or settle the argument the normal way?

Choice A: Wear the Charms
Choice B: Settle It the Normal Way

CHOICE A: WEAR THE CHARMS
First popup: They put the little bags round their necks, feeling silly, and go to sleep in their own huts. The herbs smell of mint and burnt hair. In the night, both of them dream of walking down to the stream with a heavy pot...

Ending A1 -- EACH OTHER'S SIDE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent)
In the morning (name1) wakes up in (name2)'s hut, in (name2)'s body. (Name2) wakes up in (name1)'s. The charm worked exactly as the scroll said. They are now seeing it from each other's side completely. (Apprentice name) looks at the smudge for a long time, then goes very pale. The healers try everything. Nothing undoes it. The argument about the water stops, though.

Ending A2 -- THE JOBS AS WELL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent); each now likes the thing the other liked best
They wake up in each other's bodies, and, stranger still, each liking the thing the other always loved best. (Name1) is suddenly mad about (name2)'s favourite pastime, and (name2) about (name1)'s, which, since they are now in each other's bodies, works out very neatly. "It's almost as if nothing happened," says (name2) in (name1)'s voice. "Except everything did."

CHOICE B: SETTLE IT THE NORMAL WAY
First popup: "We'll sort it out ourselves," says (name1). (Name2) agrees, for once. They sit down by the fire with a pile of shells to make a rota, which immediately starts a new argument about how many shells a day is worth...

Ending B1 -- THE ROTA. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name1) and (name2) each lose one dislike (at random)
It takes until midnight, but they come up with a rota that's fair, and then, being very tired, they laugh about the whole thing for an hour. After that they get along much better, and both of them find they mind fetching water a lot less now that it's settled.

Ending B2 -- THE APPRENTICE'S TURN. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (apprentice name) is INJURED (loses health)
They give the charms back to (apprentice name), who, rather than waste them, puts both on (himself/herself) to see what happens. Nothing happens, except that the two charms seem to argue with each other, and (apprentice name) spends the night feeling pulled in two directions and wakes up with a very bad headache and a nosebleed. The healers take the scroll away.

B154. The Memory Moths   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
Every few years, on hot nights, pale grey moths come up out of the jungle in clouds and gather round the cooking fires. The elders call them memory moths. They say the moths drink small memories the way other moths drink nectar: where someone left a knife, what they had for breakfast. Usually that's all.
Tonight there are more moths than anyone has ever seen. They are crowding round (name)'s head, so thick that (he/she) can feel their wings on (his/her) eyelids and hear them whispering, a dry papery sound like someone turning leaves. One lands on (his/her) lips.
Should (name) stay still and let them drink, or run to the sea and duck under?

Choice A: Stay Still
Choice B: Run to the Sea

CHOICE A: STAY STILL
First popup: (Name) closes (his/her) eyes and stands very still. The moths settle on (his/her) face and hair like a grey veil. (He/She) feels them drinking, small cold tugs, one after another, and tries to think about something unimportant...

Ending A1 -- THE NAME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name) LOSES NAME (name becomes "?"), drunk by the memory moths
The moths drink, and drink, and when they lift off and drift away into the dark, (name) opens (his/her) eyes and can't remember what (he/she) is called. Nor can anyone else. The moths have drunk the name out of everyone round the fire at once. They try every name they know, but none of them fits. The village calls (him/her) "?" from then on.

Ending A2 -- THE NEW ONE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: CHANGES NAME (to a random default name)
The moths drink (name)'s name, and then, very gently, one of them brushes (his/her) lips again and leaves another one behind, like a moth leaving pollen from another flower. In the morning, everyone calls (him/her) (new name), and nobody can remember (him/her) ever being called anything else. Only (name) knows something has changed, and (he/she) can't remember what.

CHOICE B: RUN TO THE SEA
First popup: (Name) runs, flapping at the moths, down the path to the beach, and wades in up to (his/her) chest and ducks under. The moths hover over the water in a grey cloud, waiting...

Ending B1 -- THE BREAKFAST. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The moths wait until (name) comes up for air, then give up and drift off to the fires again. (Name) walks home dripping and fine, apart from not remembering what (he/she) had for breakfast, or where (he/she) left (his/her) knife. (He/She) finds the knife three days later, in the cooking pot.

Ending B2 -- THE COLD WATER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name) has an ILLNESS (needs the healers)
The moths wait, and wait, and (name) stays under the water as long as (he/she) can, again and again, until the moths finally give up near dawn. (Name) walks home shivering so hard (his/her) teeth knock together. By noon (he/she) has a fever and a cough. But (he/she) still has (his/her) name.

EVENT TEXT

(Name) has never worn it. It sits in a basket by (his/her) bed. This morning, for the first time, (he/she) picks it up and runs it through (his/her) hair, and feels it pulling, gently, as if it remembers someone else's.

Choice B: Put It Back

Ending B2 -- THE STORY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

Choice B: Wait for the Ladder

CHOICE A: CLIMB DOWN

The stones give way all at once. The rope holds, but the wall of the well comes down on top of (name). The village digs all afternoon. They get the goat out alive, filthy and furious. (Name) they carry home on a door. They fill in the old well that week, every stone, and plant a fig tree on top of it, and the goat lives to a great age and won't go near it.

B157. The Brother Who Came Back   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 18 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT

Behind him in the canoe sit a tired woman, a tall teenage boy and a little girl, all staring at the village with wide eyes. "I said I'd be back," he says, a little sheepishly. "I didn't say when."
(Name) doesn't know whether to hug him or hit him. Which should (he/she) do?

Choice A: Hug Him
Choice B: Ask Where He's Been

CHOICE A: HUG HIM
First popup: (Name) grabs him and holds on, hard. He smells of salt and strange spices. His wife climbs out of the canoe, smiling uncertainly. The little girl hides behind her mother's legs...

(Name) teaches the children everything (he/she) knows, and keeps their father's spear up in the rafters, just in case.

Ending B1 -- THE LONG STORY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW VILLAGER (an adult) arrives and stays; tech gain (small amount)

By the time he finishes, the whole village has gathered round, and the researchers are writing things down as fast as they can. His family goes on to her island, but he stays, with his stories. Ending B2 -- STILL ANGRY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
He tells (name) everything, and (name) is still angry at the end of it. The brother nods. He says he understands. B177. The Shared Gourd   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: two villagers aged 14 or older (not protected), (name1) and (name2)
EVENT TEXT
At the top of the mountain there is a spring that the elders call the Spring of Understanding. They say that two people who drink from it out of the same gourd will "understand each other completely." Couples go up there. Friends go up there. Every so often, two people go up there and come down very strangely.
(Name1) and (name2) have climbed up together on a dare, sweating and laughing, with one gourd between them. Now they are standing at the spring, and it is very quiet, and the water is so clear it seems not to be there at all.
Should they drink from the same gourd, or each drink from their own hands?

Choice A: Share the Gourd
Choice B: Drink From Their Own Hands

CHOICE A: SHARE THE GOURD
First popup: (Name1) fills the gourd and drinks half, and hands it to (name2), who drinks the rest. The water tastes of cold stone and nothing else. They look at each other, waiting for something...

Ending A1 -- COMPLETELY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent)
They understand each other completely. From the inside. (Name1) is looking out of (name2)'s eyes, and (name2) is looking out of (name1)'s, and both of them sit down on the rock very suddenly. "Oh," says (name2), in (name1)'s voice. "That's what they meant by strangely." They walk down the mountain very slowly, in each other's legs. There is no undoing it.

Ending A2 -- COMPLETELY, AND THEN SOME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent); each loses one dislike (at random)
They swap bodies, and with that, they understand exactly why the other one is the way they are: the aches, the habits, the small fears. By the bottom of the mountain they are calmer than either has ever been. "I'm sorry about the knee," says (name1). "I'm sorry about the stomach," says (name2). A few things that used to bother them stop bothering them.

CHOICE B: DRINK FROM THEIR OWN HANDS
First popup: "Let's not be silly," says (name2). They kneel at the spring and drink out of their own cupped hands, side by side, and sit back on their heels...

Ending B1 -- NOTHING AT ALL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The water is cold and clean and nothing happens. They sit by the spring as the sun goes down, talking about nothing much, and walk down in the dark, still talking. It turns out they understand each other a lot better than they thought, without any help.

Ending B2 -- THE FALL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name1) is INJURED (loses health)

(Name2) climbs down after (name1: him/her) and carries (name1: him/her) the rest of the way on (name2: his/her) back, which takes all night. They understand each other completely by morning, without the spring.

B179. The Fern That Remembers   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]

EVENT TEXT

Choice B: Take It to the Healers

Ending A1 -- CURLED BACK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name) gets the young head look
By the time (name) gets home, (his/her) face has curled back fifteen years. Smooth skin, bright eyes, not a line on (him/her). The rest of (him/her) is the same age as before. (Healer name) looks at (him/her) for a long time. "Unpredictable," (he/she) says. "But I'll admit it suits you."

Ending A2 -- THE RASH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name) is INJURED (loses health)

CHOICE B: TAKE IT TO THE HEALERS

Ending B1 -- THE SMOKE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name) gets the "old" head look

Ending B2 -- STORED SAFELY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: every healer gains 5 Healing
The frond lands on the edge of the fire and (healer name) snatches it out before it can catch. B190. The Crab Moon   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: two villagers aged 14 or older (not protected), (name1) and (name2)
EVENT TEXT
Once a year, under the full moon, the land crabs march down from the jungle to the sea, thousands of them, clicking and scraping across the village in a red tide. The elders say it's bad luck to step on one, and worse luck to be caught in the middle of the march, because the crabs "carry people's spirits back and forth in their claws, and don't always put them back where they found them."
(Name1) and (name2) were walking home late and have been caught on the path, right in the middle of the march. Crabs are everywhere, around their feet, climbing over their toes. There's nowhere to put a foot down.
Should they stand still and wait for the crabs to pass, or run for it?

Choice A: Stand Still
Choice B: Run for It

CHOICE A: STAND STILL
First popup: They stand back to back in the moonlight, not moving, while the crabs flow round their ankles like water. Clicking. Scraping. Hundreds of little eyes on stalks, all turned towards them...

Ending A1 -- PUT BACK WRONG. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent)
The march takes an hour to pass. At some point in that hour, standing back to back, they both feel a pinch, very gently, at the back of the neck. When the last crab has gone, (name1) turns round and sees (name1: his/her) own face looking back. The crabs have put them back, but in the wrong places. The elders aren't surprised. "Never be in the middle," they say.

Ending A2 -- THE PINCH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The crabs flow past for an hour, and one of them gives (name2) a sharp pinch on the toe on its way, which (name2) says is extremely rude. Otherwise nothing happens. When the march has passed, they walk home along a path scraped clean, and (name2) limps a little, and complains about the crab the whole way.

CHOICE B: RUN FOR IT
First popup: "Run!" shouts (name2), and they run, hopping and leaping, trying to land in the gaps. Crabs crunch under their feet. Both of them wince at every one...

Ending B1 -- ANGRY CRABS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent); (name1) and (name2) are INJURED (pinched all over; lose health)
The crabs take it personally. They swarm up the two of them, pinching, until they fall down in a heap together, covered. When the march has passed, each of them is lying in the other's body, pinched all over. "That's what you get for stepping on them," say the elders, putting cool mud on the pinches. There is no putting them back.

Ending B2 -- HOME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name1) and (name2) each lose one dislike (at random)
They get home breathless and laughing, with crab bits on their feet, and sit on (name1)'s doorstep watching the red tide go past in the moonlight. It is, they agree, the most ridiculous thing that has ever happened to either of them. After a night like that, a lot of small things they used to grumble about don't seem worth the trouble.

B196. The Second Tide   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
Twice a year the tide goes out further than usual, much further, so far that the reef stands up out of the water and the whole lagoon is a field of wet sand and puddles. (Name) is walking across the bare lagoon floor with a basket, picking up stranded fish. In the middle of the lagoon (he/she) comes across a hollow in the sand, full of water, perfectly still, and lying in it, asleep, is someone with (his/her) own face.

"Thank you," says the sleeper, in (name)'s voice, and sits up. It is (name) exactly, the same in every way, as if the sea had been keeping a spare. It walks back across the lagoon floor beside (name) as the tide starts to turn, and into the village, and takes the name (new name). The old fishers shake their heads and say nothing at all.

Ending A2 -- NOT QUITE THE SAME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: DUPLICATE of (name), named (new name); joins the village

It doesn't like fish, it hates the sun, and it laughs at (name)'s jokes in a way that suggests it doesn't find them funny. It follows (name) home anyway, and takes the name (new name). "The sea gives back what it wants," say the old fishers. "Not what you want."

CHOICE B: LEAVE IT WHERE IT LIES
First popup: (Name) backs away, slowly, and walks on across the lagoon, not looking back. Behind (him/her), the water starts to come back in over the sand, very fast...

Ending B1 -- THE SEA TAKES IT BACK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

Ending B2 -- IT FOLLOWS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: CLONE of (name), named (new name); joins the village

B231. The Moon in the Bowl   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
On the night of the full moon, the elders say, if a bowl of seawater is set out on a flat stone and the moon is caught in it exactly in the middle, whoever looks into it will see their face the way the moon sees it. B239. The Long Night Fire   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected); the rest of the village
EVENT TEXT
On the longest night of the year, the village keeps the big fire burning till dawn, and everyone takes turns telling what they are best at, and teaching it to anyone who wants to listen. The elders say the long night fire "makes skills take root." This year (name) has been chosen to keep the fire going all night, alone, while the others talk and learn and fall asleep around it.
At midnight, the wood pile is running low, and the rain has started. (Name) can go into the dark jungle for more dry wood, or start burning the village's spare roof thatch, which the builders will be furious about.
Which should (name) do?

Choice A: Go for Wood
Choice B: Burn the Spare Thatch

CHOICE A: GO FOR WOOD
First popup: (Name) wraps up against the rain and goes into the dark jungle with an axe, feeling for dry branches under the big trees, while behind (him/her) the fire sinks lower and lower...

Ending A1 -- THE FIRE HOLDS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: every villager gains 5 in their best skill; (name) gains 10 to 20 in (his/her) best skill
(Name) comes back with an armful of dry wood just as the fire is about to go out, and builds it up roaring. All night the villagers teach each other round it, and by dawn every one of them has learned something from someone. (Name), who stayed up all night listening to all of it, has learned the most.

Ending A2 -- THE FIRE GOES OUT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (name) is INJURED (loses health)
In the dark, (name) trips over a root and falls on the axe handle and cracks a rib. By the time (he/she) limps back with the wood, the fire is out and everyone has gone to bed. Nobody blames (him/her), but the elders say the skills won't take root this year. (Name) spends a week in the healers' hut.

CHOICE B: BURN THE SPARE THATCH
First popup: (Name) drags the bundles of spare thatch out of the store and feeds them to the fire one by one. The fire flares up bright and hot and crackling, and the builders, asleep, don't notice...

Ending B1 -- A BRIGHT NIGHT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: every villager gains 5 in their best skill
The thatch burns so bright that nobody falls asleep, and the teaching goes on till dawn, and every villager comes away better at something. Then the builders wake up and find the spare thatch gone. (Builder name) doesn't speak to (name) for a week. It was, everyone else agrees, worth it.

Ending B2 -- THE SPARK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: every villager gains 5 in their best skill; tech loss (small amount)
The thatch burns very bright, and a burning wisp flies up on the wind and lands on the roof of the research hut. It's put out in moments, but not before a season of notes has gone up. The long night still does its work: every villager learns something by dawn. The researchers learn the most, about where to keep their notes. Your villagers lose (award) tech points.

They want to trade for the village's own seeds, and for "something to wear that we haven't got."
(Name) has been sent to do the trading. The traders' grandmother, who does all the talking, is looking at (name)'s clothes with great interest. The grandmother's grandson, a tall teenager, is looking at the village as if he'd like to stay.
Should (name) trade (his/her) clothes for the rarest seeds, or trade the village's spare seeds?

Choice B: Trade the Village's Seeds

Ending B1 -- A GOOD TRADE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (small amount)

In the morning, the grandmother sails on with one canoe, and her son, his wife and the tall grandson stay with the other, to plant the new seeds and see them grow. "Somebody has to," the grandmother says.

  death                   19 / 16

  nursing                 26 / 19

  old look                18 / 13
  illness cured           34 / 15
  huts repaired           28 / 19
  group effects           30 / 17
  best skill              33 / 18

  permanent disability    17 / 15
  like removed            27 / 20
  dislike removed         29 / 17
  everyone happier        22 / 12
  tech loss                6 / 3
  total 485
Notes:
- An ending that carries two quota effects counts once for each.
- "group effects" counts every-villager / every-healer / every-builder / every-fisher / every-elder / N random villagers lines
  (not "every villager is happier", which is counted on its own row).
- "old look" counts only the "old" head look given on its own, not the one that comes with a permanent disability.
- "family arrivals" counts NEW VILLAGERS lines and single adult, teen, child or elder arrivals; found babies count under nursing.
- Every kind reached its share. Every event carries at least two quota endings (as the brief asks), so most kinds are
  over; the biggest overshoots are illness cured (+19), best skill (+15), group effects (+13), dislike removed (+12),
  huts repaired (+9), young look (+8) and everyone happier (+10). Tech loss is 6 against a share of 3.
- Like removals use only words that change behaviour somewhere (running, work, learning, playing, jumping, rain,
  laundry, eating); the line says which games, and "eating" works only in VV2.

BALANCE EVENTS B241-B360 (120 new island events, static + mixer seed) -- draft for the owner, 2026-11-16
Written to even out the outcome kinds (BALANCE_BRIEF.md), in the owner's style guide. NOT in the patcher.
- Layout and conventions as OWNER_EDITED_315.txt. Every ending within a choice is equally likely.
- Like/dislike EFFECTs use each game's own word (likes_dislikes.json); "story only" marks games where the word does nothing.
- Twins/triplets and two-clone endings use the count tokens {#babies:...} and {#made:...} (rule 13).
- Pregnancy carriers are born female, 18+, unless marked (ANY BIRTH SEX) for magic or a found baby. VV5: newcomers are Isolans.

B241. The Night the Roofs Flew   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected); (builder name), the village's best builder
EVENT TEXT
The wind came in off the sea just after dark and did not stop until dawn. It howled through the palms, rattled every door, and pulled the thatch off three huts as easily as someone peeling a banana. In the grey morning light the village looks plucked. Bundles of thatch hang in the trees. One roof is sitting, almost whole, in the middle of the taro patch.
(Name) stands with (builder name), the village's best builder, looking at the bare rafters. "We could fix it all today if everyone helps," (builder name) says, "or we wait for the ground to dry and do it properly. Wet thatch rots."
Should (name) gather the whole village now, or wait for dry weather?

Choice A: Gather Everyone Now
Choice B: Wait for Dry Weather

CHOICE A: GATHER EVERYONE NOW
First popup: (Name) walks from hut to hut, knocking on doors that are still standing and calling into the ones that aren't. Soon there is a line of villagers passing thatch up ladders, and (builder name) is shouting directions from a rooftop...

Ending A1 -- MANY HANDS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: the damaged huts are repaired (stock island-event effect); every builder gains 5 Building
By sunset every roof is back on. Some of them are a little lumpy, and one has a coconut stuck in it that nobody can get out, but none of them leak. The builders, who did most of the shouting, learned more in one day than in a season of ordinary work. (Builder name) climbs down last, stiff and sunburnt, and declares the coconut "structural."

Ending A2 -- THE TARO PATCH ROOF. Chance 50%. EFFECT: the damaged huts are repaired (stock island-event effect); every villager is happier (stock island-event effect)
The roof in the taro patch turns out to be in such good shape that eight people simply pick it up and carry it back, singing a work song in time with their steps. It drops onto its old hut with a thump and fits perfectly. Everyone cheers so loudly that the pigs run off. That night the village eats together under the newly mended roofs, sore-armed and proud.

CHOICE B: WAIT FOR DRY WEATHER
First popup: "Properly, then," says (name). The families with no roofs squeeze in with neighbours, and everyone waits for the sun, which takes its time...

Ending B1 -- THREE DRY DAYS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: the damaged huts are repaired (stock island-event effect); (builder name) gains 10 in (his/her) best skill
The sun comes out on the third day and stays. (Builder name) re-thatches every roof with dry, tight bundles, tied the way (his/her) grandmother taught (him/her), and the new roofs are better than the old ones ever were. People keep stopping to look up at them. "That," says (builder name), "is what waiting gets you."

Ending B2 -- THE LONG DRIZZLE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
It drizzles for a week. Nobody gets any sleep, because every hut that still has a roof now has two families in it, and somebody in every family snores. By the time the thatch is dry enough to use, people have started fixing their own roofs with whatever they can find. The village ends up with three roofs that look like birds' nests, and a great many opinions about whose fault that is.

WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
(Name) is mending a net on the beach when (he/she) notices a canoe drifting just outside the reef. Its sail is torn to ribbons and it sits low in the water. Someone in it is waving a paddle over their head, slowly, as if they have been waving for a long time. (Name) can see at least three people, maybe more.
The reef is sharp and the tide is turning. Swimming out is dangerous. The canoe might drift in on its own, or it might drift right past the island.
Should (name) swim out to them, or run and light a signal fire so they can steer for the gap in the reef?

Choice A: Swim Out to Them
Choice B: Light a Signal Fire

CHOICE A: SWIM OUT TO THEM
First popup: (Name) drops the net, wades in and starts swimming. The water over the reef is choppy and full of churned sand, and (he/she) has to pick (his/her) way carefully between the coral heads...

(Name) reaches the canoe and finds a young couple, sunburnt and cracked-lipped, with a baby tucked in a dry basket between them. They have been at sea for nine days, since a storm blew them off course. (Name) takes the bow line in (his/her) teeth and guides them through the gap in the reef. (Name) brings them in, bleeding the whole way, and has to be helped up the beach. The teenager stays by (his/her) side until the healers come.

Ending B1 -- THEY SEE IT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW VILLAGERS (two adults) arrive with their baby (in New Believers they are Isolans)

"We followed your smoke," they say, and they never leave.

Ending B2 -- TOO FAR. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

(He/She) keeps the fire burning all night anyway. In the morning there is nothing on the horizon. (Name) tells (himself/herself) that the next island over has beaches too, and tries to believe it.

B251. The Lightning Under the Banyan   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: two villagers aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT

The pot holds something that smells like a burnt goat. (Healer name) makes them both breathe it in at the same time. They sneeze at the same moment, and when they open their eyes, they are back where they belong. CHOICE B: FIX IT THEMSELVES

Ending B1 -- THE STORM MOVES ON. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent); both lose the dislike of lifting (acts in VV3 and VV4; story only in VV1, VV2 and VV5)
The storm moves out to sea without another strike. They wait until dark, soaked and shivering, and then trudge home. Living each other's lives turns out to be the only way to settle the argument. By the end of the month, each of them has carried the other's water jar up from the stream so many times that the fetching and carrying they both used to dread doesn't bother either of them any more. They stop arguing, and they never swap back.

Ending B2 -- STRUCK AGAIN. Chance 50%. EFFECT: body swap, then swapped back (no lasting change); both lose health

B352. The Moon Bath   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]

The trick, the elders say, is to bathe facing the moon, never with one's back to it.
It's midnight. (Name) is standing waist-deep in the silver light, and has just realised (he/she) doesn't know which way is which. Should (name) turn and face the moon, or stay as (he/she) is and duck under?

(His/her) face is the one (he/she) had at twenty, though nothing else has changed. "Facing the moon," (name) says, very pleased with (himself/herself). "It's all in the facing."

...and nothing happens. The cough is still there in the morning. And the taste of that much honey, all at once, has put (name) off sweet things, and then off food of almost any kind, for a very long time. (Healer name) gives (him/her) the usual bitter root instead, which works in three days, and tastes like a wet boot.

B360. The Ghost in the Empty Hut   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
The hut at the end of the row has been empty for a year, since its last family moved to the far side of the island, and it has started to fall apart: the roof sags, the walls lean, and at night, people say, someone inside it hums. The elders say a hut that is left empty too long gets lonely and calls for someone to fix it.
(Name) walks past it at dusk and hears the humming. It's a sad, tuneless sort of hum. Should (name) go inside, or fetch the builders in the morning to see to it?

Choice A: Go Inside
Choice B: Fetch the Builders in the Morning

CHOICE A: GO INSIDE
First popup: (Name) pushes the sagging door open. Inside it is dark and smells of old thatch. The humming stops. Something brushes past (his/her) face, cool as a breath...

Ending A1 -- THE HUT'S FACE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW LOOK (a new head look)
Then the humming starts again, much happier, right beside (name)'s ear. (Name) runs. In the morning, (his/her) face in the water jar is different: still (his/hers), but shaped a little like the faces carved on the old hut's doorposts. The elders say the hut has said thank you for the visit. (Name) wishes it had said it in words.

Ending A2 -- THE HUT IS MENDED. Chance 50%. EFFECT: the damaged huts are repaired (stock island-event effect)
In the dark, (name) finds the problem at once: a cracked ridgepole, sagging in the middle, creaking in the wind with a sound exactly like humming. (He/She) fetches the builders in the morning anyway, and while they are mending the empty hut, they find three more with cracked ridgepoles, and mend those too. Nobody hears the humming again.

CHOICE B: FETCH THE BUILDERS IN THE MORNING
First popup: (Name) goes home and sleeps badly. In the morning, (he/she) brings the builders, and they stand outside the empty hut listening. The humming is still there, in broad daylight...

Ending B1 -- A NEW FAMILY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: the damaged huts are repaired (stock island-event effect); NEW VILLAGERS (two adults) arrive with their baby (in New Believers they are Isolans)
The builders mend the hut, and every other hut that needs it on the way. The very next week, a young couple with a baby come over the hill, looking for somewhere to live. The empty hut is ready for them, and they move straight in. That night, from inside, (name) hears a happy, tuneful sort of humming: the baby's parent, singing to the baby.

Ending B2 -- THE BIRD'S NEST. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The humming is a pair of nesting doves in the rafters, who have been cooing to each other all year. The builders mend the hut around them, carefully, leaving the nest where it is. The doves stay. The hut stays empty. But nobody calls it haunted any more, and the children go and listen to the doves on the way home.
